speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman) had an opportunity to make his speech, and now the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Mr. Young) has the floor.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
I wonder whether the hon. member would care to consult with some of his Tory colleagues in New Brunswick who show only passing lip service to environmental concern in the onslaught against natural resources.
I wish to take a few minutes to deal with the remarks made by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent. It seems that members opposite have an almost holier-than-thou attitude toward the James Bay agreement and this legislation. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent said that he did not want to see the federal government continue a paternalistic attitude toward the native people. However, he and his colleagues suggest that they know better than the native people who have been involved in these negotiations for the rights, details and the land use that they want. He overlooks the fact that the whole emphasis of the agreement and the whole purpose of this legislation are to allow the native people to become independent and as autonomous as possible, to preserve and enhance a culture, and allow the Cree and Inuit to develop at their own pace.
This legislation will ensure that these people can develop at their own pace. The Inuit and Cree will be the decision makers of their own future. They will become a self-determining, self-governing people. This legislation will put aside the old paternalistic policies and programs.
It was not until the development of the James Bay region that the native people learned that they were going to have to do this, but necessity is the mother of invention. The needs of the native people have been brought to the fore. Out of those pressing needs that they felt, their concern for their lands, their traditional territories, and these negotiations, they have been able to make enormous strides in their own growth.
The hon. member for Lambton-Kent seemed to put forward the idea that the agreement would be continuing a policy of paternalism. I talked to some of these native people recently. I also talked to a number of the executive of the Grand Council of the Cree. They told me how much they have been able to mature and how they have become decision makers in their own right. They tell me how happy they are to have been able to bargain for themselves. They now feel that the Cree are the ones who are dealing with the question of Cree rights. All the native people feel they are able to use this agreement to get what they want.
I believe history will record that the federal government did the native people a tremendous service in enabling them to

express their wishes, to fight for this arrangement and to show their spirit of pride in their accomplishments.
Last evening the hon. member for Lambton-Kent gave the impression that it was the federal government which imposed all the deadlines. I am told by members of the Grand Council of Cree that they were the ones who imposed the November 1, 1975, deadline for reaching a final agreement. Agreement in principle had been reached about a year earlier. It was the Cree who gave an ultimatum to Quebec to sign by November 1. They said to the province, "Sign, or we are going home; we have talked enough; let us put up or shut up." The native people wanted to get on with the job. The hon. member spoke of the short period in which the vote was taken. He did not explain that the period of preparation for ratification ran from November, 1975, to March, 1976.
It is important to realize the purpose of the agreement and of the legislation from the point of view of the Cree and the Inuit. They had it in mind that through this vehicle they could rid themselves of poverty and of dependence on the hand-out system; that they could build their own houses and maintain their traditional way of life. I am told that many benefits of the agreement have already begun to show up in these areas. I am told by the Grand Council of the Cree that over two thirds of the Cree people are practising their traditional way of life. They are not being assimilated. They feel the policy of alert neutrality on the part of the federal government was one of the best which could have been followed in their case. It led to the formation of the Grand Council and to decisions being taken at the grass roots. Native people have begun to decide what is best for native people.
I am told that one of the first instructions the native leaders received from their bands was to negotiate in three areas, land; fishing, hunting and trapping rights; and the question of changes in the project. But in the course of the negotiations the Cree and the Inuit soon realized that they could go much further, that they could take over other fields such as education, health services, housing, and so on. In essence they could begin to look after all the day to day decision-making processes which so closely affect their communities. More power to them.
If my understanding is correct, about two years ago members of the Conservative party and some members of the New Democratic Party were saying to us on this side of the House, "Tell the Cree not to go to court; tell them they should resort to negotiation and try to work out a deal for themselves." Today, when an agreement has been signed and when legislation is before the House, they are not happy with the situation. Indeed they are saying the Indians should not have negotiated, that they have not done well enough out of it.
Again, from conversations I have had in recent days with members of the Cree Grand Council I find they do not feel they were ever left out, or held at the point of a gun. As a matter of fact one council member said to me, and this is a direct quotation, "We feel we have the tomahawk in our
December 8, 1976

hands." The Indians felt that it was they who had set many of the deadlines and conditions. Conversely, I know there are some in the province of Quebec who feel the native people were able to get too much, and now they are beginning to have second thoughts.
I do not believe the native people got too much. They got what they were there for. They had to make compromises, of course. They realize that all their demands could not be satisfied. But my impression is that they are happy with the outcome. They have developed. They have gone a long way toward getting what they wanted in the first place. They are able to set their own policies and make their own decisions.
In the minds of the native people, comments like those made by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent and the hon. member for Fraser Valley West will, I fear, give the impression to the native people that Ottawa is against their negotiating and developing their own governmental systems. Many of those people do not look on this chamber, in Ottawa, as being composed of members from one party or another; they do not always see the difference between Conservatives, Liberals, and members of the NDP. They look on Ottawa as a monolith. I am afraid that some of the benefits which will flow from this legislation might be lost as a result of comments such as we have heard from the other side. The native people have learned the necessity for compromise. They learned that not everybody can be entirely satisfied. But they tell me they can live with what they now have and that their primary interests are protected.
Let me comment further on what was said in the debate by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent. He stated, if I recall correctly, that all the documents were in French and that all the negotiations were carried out in French. According to my understanding, this is incorrect. I am told that everything was negotiated in English and that all the documents were prepared in English, even the working papers and discussion notes, with the exception of one brief paper which came from the Quebec department of Justice, which was in the French language. The documents which were prepared in English were taken back to the bands, to the native communities, and translated at band council meetings by the negotiators themselves. They were carried back, explained and translated by the Cree, and I understand that a similar process was undertaken in the case of the Inuit people.
I do not hear complaints of any hassles on that score when these things are explained to me. It is true there are complications attached to translating and explaining the details of lengthy and complicated agreements. I sometimes wonder how much any of us understand with respect to the detail of legislative items which appear before us. I suggest that very few of us at any time are truly conversant with such details. On the other hand, most of us have gone through our own translation process here. Most of us have a good general idea of what the legislation we pass will do, together with some specifics.
The general sense of this agreement, the main principles, were fully translated and understood by the people back in the
James Bay Agreement
settlements. I understand that the decision to accept the final proposals was taken at local levels and brought back to the negotiating table while work was done on the over-all agreement.
Last evening the hon. member asked some questions about the Naskapi. I understand that the Naskapi could have been included in the final agreement but that they decided on their own not to sign the agreement in principle. It was not a case of the federal government keeping the Naskapi out. It was, rather, the Naskapi themselves who decided they were not ready. Their decision was respected by the government. They were left out by their own desire and not because of any action on the part of the federal government. The Naskapi position was respected by the federal government. They themselves felt they were not ready at that time. Since then they have been organizing and negotiating to be brought into the agreement and to derive the same benefits along with the Inuit and the Cree. Bill C-9 will provide for this as well. It provides for room to enter into agreement with the terms and conditions they like.
There will be further developments as a result of this legislation, and it may very well be in the future that many of the powers the federal ministry now holds will be turned over to the Indian peoples. This is designed to end the paternalism of earlier days, to allow them to become self-determining and self-governing. The agreement and legislation are designed, and here I use the exact words of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, "to allow them the opportunity to grow and develop on their own". The agreement will give them this opportunity not only to grow and develop, but to do so at their own pace, not one set for them by a provincial or federal government.
I had a very interesting conversation with Chief Billy Diamond. One of the things he said which struck me most was that as a Cree he believes that being an Indian is just not enough any more. He believes that the benefits of the agreement and the legislation will give him and his people the opportunity to reinforce their identity. It will allow them to become masters of their own destiny and of their own plans.
Last evening the hon. member for Lambton-Kent said it was not possible to set out a master plan for evolution. I do not think anyone could do that because things are never static, they change from day to day. However, the agreement takes that into account and leaves room for change. It can be redefined and reorganized with the agreement and consent of all parties to better meet the needs of the native people as they themselves grow and develop. With this legislation the opportunity to grow and develop becomes possible, and the opportunity becomes theirs. If there is no agreement and no legislation, the native people see a rather dark future in which they will continue to be overwhelmed by the trespassers of their traditional lands; by the developers of gigantic projects. The agreement and the legislation are going to prevent that from happening.
1794

December 8, 1976
James Bay Agreement
The native people will be the ones to participate in decisions regarding their own developments. I think that is the essence of this. I am happy to see this kind of legislation before the House. I am even more happy to sense the spirit of accomplishment, maturity and development the native people feel within themselves. Now is their chance. They can develop, they can define their own programs and their own growth and needs. I think they have long deserved this chance. It is about time we stopped trying to tell them how to do things and gave them the opportunity to develop and do things for themselves. I welcome the agreement, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I have to say this afternoon might not be well received by some of my Indian friends. My reputation as a parliamentarian and as a worker for the Indian cause is well established, and I can call them friends.
I do not like the James Bay agreement. I am disappointed in the early result of our effort to recognize the principle and concept of aboriginal title which only occurred about two years ago. The James Bay agreement is probably the first of its kind and one of many agreements that will have to be worked out with our brothers throughout the country.
I represent an area in western Canada almost as large as the area affected by this agreement. I am afraid I would have to fight to the bitter end before seeing a similar agreement or situation perpetrated on my native friends in my constituency.
The leaders who are urging us to activate this agreement by passing this bill have, in my opinion, not considered the long-range implications and effects of what they have signed. Their eyes have been blinded by a promise of instant wealth and prosperity, and long-range guarantees which are no more valid in this agreement than they were in treaties which their forefathers signed 100 years ago. The difference is that this agreement, if in fact it is legal, which I doubt, constitutes a sellout of the birthright of our indigenous people in this country, and that includes the birthright of generations not yet born.
I understand all the human factors involved. I know what it is like to anticipate. I understand how they feel; being on welfare for five generations; being a member of a family of five and each will receive $10,000, which is just around the corner and all that is holding it up is the passage of this bill in the House of Commons. I understand all that. This would amount to $50,000. Just imagine what it will do. It will buy a brand new house, two new ski-doos, and all the things the people have always wanted for their families and loved ones.
What happens, Mr. Speaker, when the new house needs repairs and the ski-doos have run out of gas? What happens after the years have passed and new generations have come along and want to cash in on their birthright?
Let me talk a little bit about the area that is to be affected. The James Bay agreement represents the surrender of native rights over a huge territory which Indians have been using and occupying fully since time immemorial. It extinguishes all native land claims in Quebec north of the fifty-fifth parallel,

and any south of that arising from the project. The James Bay development projects will affect drainage areas stretching from a point 200 miles north of Montreal up to Ungava Bay, a distance of 1,000 miles.
The agreement affects roughly 10,000 people; 6,500 Cree Indians and 3,500 Inuit. In addition, of course, there is an unidentified number of others who can and have been designated as non-status and Metis. In modern terms they have been identified as the forgotten people. They have been identified in that way because the provincial and federal governments have forgotten that they exist. I am afraid now that some of their own brothers may have forgotten that they live in the area as well and should have their interests protected.
For the most part this population in northern Quebec has maintained a traditional way of life in which the main economic pursuits are fishing, hunting and trapping. This native lifestyle has as its elements freedom to move over ancestral lands, to use these lands fully, and to maintain an identity, culture and language. Both Indians and Inuit are recognized as special federal responsibilities under section 91(24) of the British North America Act. This section specifies that the federal government is responsible for Indians and lands reserved for Indians, the designation "Indians" being extended by a later Supreme Court decision to include the Inuit as well. Responsibility has also been interpreted by subsequent court decisions to include lands occupied and used by Indians which are not necessarily reserves as defined by treaties or the Indian Act. Responsibility for Indians, moreover, is taken by most legal experts to mean Indians wherever they may happen to live; on reserves or away from them.
Although the applicability of section 91(24) to non-status Indians and Metis has never been the subject of a court decision, there are legal grounds for believing that this constitutional reference would be found to apply. There are grounds, therefore, for arguing that non-status and Metis people also have a stake in special status as one of their future options. Given this possibility, they should have a legitimate cause for concern if the actions of a province or the federal government had the effect of forever closing the door on such an option. The James Bay settlement in effect does this very thing in northern Quebec. The principle of native title is well established. As a matter of fact I question the constitutionality of this agreement on the following grounds, namely, the principles established by the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912 and other similar acts, and a variety of court decisions upholding the British North America Act in subsequent years.
Let me review briefly, Mr. Speaker, the legal proceedings leading to the James Bay agreement. In May, 1972, the Crees and Inuit of northern Quebec launched a court action to have Bill 50, which was an act respecting the development of the James Bay area, declared unconstitutional. They asked for a permanent order of injunction to halt all work on the James Bay project. The action was taken against the James Bay Development Corporation, the James Bay Energy Corpora-
December 8, 1976

tion, Hydro-Quebec, and a number of other contractors engaged in the project. The hearings on the petition began in November, 1972, and lasted till June, 1973.
The basic native position was that they had territorial rights in those areas which would be affected by the development. It was argued that these rights were reflected in the terms of the statute of 1912, the Quebec Northern Boundaries Extension Act, which transferred a part of the territory to Quebec. This act stipulated that:
. .. the Province of Quebec will recognize the rights of the Indian inhabitants in the territory above described to the same extent, and will obtain surrenders of such rights in the same manner, as the Government of Canada has heretofore recognized such rights and has obtained surrender thereof, and the said Province shall hear and satisfy all charges and expenditures in connection with or arising out of such surrenders.
The southern part of the James Bay area had been transferred to Quebec in 1898 without any undertakings from the province to recognize native rights. Nevertheless, the native people claimed rights in this particular territory, too. They referred to an Imperial Order-in-Council transferring Ruperts Land from the Hudson's Bay Company to Canada; a federal order in council of May 2, 1910, which commented on a January 17, 1910, order in council and stated that the act of 1898 did not give any land to the province of Quebec free from the burden of Indian title; the Dominion Lands Acts which stipulated that none of the provisions of these acts applied to territories where Indian title was not extinguished; and treaty making as a policy of the federal government was held to be a clear recognition of aboriginal title. Of course, Mr. Speaker, all of their arguments were valid and well founded.
The native people claimed that the James Bay development was resulting in substantial harm and disruption to their way of life. They insisted, moreover, that they had never surrendered their rights, and therefore the lands in question belonged to them and could not be used without prior agreement.
On November 15, 1973, Mr. Justice Malouf of the Superior Court of Quebec heard the case and ruled in favour of the native people's position. The judge held that since the native people of James Bay had never signed treaties ceding their land, they had rights to the land, including the right to fish, hunt and trap there. He considered the question of the "balance of convenience" on which the various development corporations placed great emphasis in putting forth their case. In effect, they argued that there would be great monetary loss suffered by them if work was stopped in midstream. The judge rejected this argument because he believed it would establish an unusual principle in dealings with native people; it would permit a person to change the status quo prior to or pending a court hearing and subsequently plead "balance of convenience". The injunction was therefore granted, ordering the developers to "cease, desist and refrain from interfering in any way with the petitioners'-native-rights, from trespassing in the said territory, and from causing damage to the environmental and natural resources of the said territory".
The case was appealed immediately. The Court of Appeal suspended Judge Maloufs order of injunction, permitting work to be resumed pending an appeal to the Supreme Court
James Bay Agreement
of Canada. The Court of Appeal, in effect, denied the principle that the rights of a weak party should be balanced against those of a strong one by accepting the "balance of convenience" doctrine. These judges believed that the inconvenience of Indians as a result of the project was less than the inconvenience of stopping the work at high cost and in the face of growing energy need in Quebec. The judges did not, of course, consider that the right way to go about this would have been to ask the Indians before the project started, so that this inconvenience would not have resulted either to the companies concerned or to the people of Quebec.
On December 21, 1973, in a three to two decision, the Supreme Court of Canada refused leave to appeal from the judgment of the Court of Appeal, thus forcing the native people to negotiate. The natives of James Bay learned, in fact, that once the project had been started in their territory there was nothing they could do to stop it. There was nothing they could do, moreover, to re-assert the rights which the construction of the project was violating. They had to negotiate- literally with a gun at their heads.
Let me talk briefly about the settlement, Mr. Speaker. On November 11, 1975, a final agreement was signed by which the native people of northern Quebec surrendered their rights to the territory forever. The agreement provides for a cash settlement and certain land rights-$225 million to be paid over many years, and retention as owners, surface title only- and that is important-of less than 2 per cent of traditionally used lands. The money does not amount to much, regardless of how anxious they are to receive it. Discounting the current cash value, it works out to about $10,000 per capita. I have to add that, of course, the words "per capita" apply only if the status Indians and Inuit are considered. However, if status Indians were to share this bounty with some of their non-status brothers, this figure of course would be reduced.
As we know, in the agreement land is divided into three categories. In category 1 the lands are those immediately surrounding the existing community. The native people affected by the agreement have exclusive right to about 5,000 square miles, representing for the most part existing communities. Exclusive rights really mean that these lands will be treated in a way similar to municipalities. When the minister leads us to believe that these lands will be treated in a way similar to existing reservations, he is, of course, misleading us. The agreement does not establish any reserves as was done under earlier treaties.
Category 2 land covers about 60,000 square miles and is available for hunting, trapping and fishing. Presumably permission to use these lands for these purposes could be gradually withdrawn, either as the native lifestyle fades over the years or when more pressing uses for this land occur.
Land in category 3 is the balance of the land and it covers around 250,000 square miles. On these lands the native people will have no rights whatsoever. The land settlement does not provide any sub-surface right in any of the categories of land.
80005-461/2

December 8, 1976
James Bay Agreement
Native people will therefore have no claim to oil or minerals already discovered or to be found.
In summary, therefore, of a total of around 315,000 square miles of territory to which the native people have rights, they have retained about 2 per cent of the land on which to live, and 25 per cent of the land on which to hunt, trap and fish. The balance of about 73 per cent has been given up for development purposes. In effect, under the agreement the province of Quebec has reorganized the territory and set up institutions and structures which are subject to provincial control only.
On June 30, 1976, bill 12 of the National Assembly of Quebec, an act approving the agreement concerning James Bay in northern Quebec, was passed. I should like to read some quotes here because the bill passed through the provincial house and some interesting statements were made there which I should like to place on the record. They were made in committee by one John Ciaccia, a former employee of the provincial government concerned with matters to do with Indians. This is what he said as he tried to steer the bill through the provincial legislature:
This means that where facilities such as schools and hospitals already exist under federal jurisdiction in native communities, they will be transferred to the jurisdiction of Quebec. In the case of certain federal programs already operating, the Quebec government will assume the responsibility for them.
The next sentence is very significant. He said:
This agreement will in fact take precedence over the federal Indian Act.
Bill C-9, the federal counterpart of Bill 32 in Quebec, has received first reading in parliament and is now before us for second reading. When it receives second reading and final approval, the James Bay agreement will be fully implemented.
Let me talk about some of the implications of the agreement. The agreement represents a regional abdication of the philosophy and intent of the federal government's White paper of 1969. The White paper was designed to terminate federal responsibility for Indians by doing away with the constitutional reference to Indians; by eliminating the Indian act; by doing away with the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development; by removing federal protection of reserve lands by turning them over to Indians in fee simple; and by transferring all program responsibilities to the provinces.
When we talk about turning over the program responsibilities to the provinces, we have to consider the fact that we are now dealing with a province which is identified is a press statement issued yesterday by the Native Council of Canada as follows:
The federal government has no right to sign over its responsibilities for the Indian and Eskimo lands in any part of Canada to a jurisdiction whose avowed goal is independence from federal authority. Previous guarantees and safeguards built into the proposed agreement are meaningless in a Quebec that may not, in the future, be part of Canada under the constitutional authority of a federal government.
We are talking about the surrendering of the federal government's responsibility for native people to a government which said publicly and as a matter of policy that any agreement with the federal government at this time will be viewed by this government as interim at best, and that they have no intention

of honouring any of these agreements once they have achieved their avowed goal. I would ask my native friends to consider that.
I too believe that this new government in Quebec may be more conscious of its social responsibilities and may be better prepared to respond to the special needs of my native friends. But who are we dealing with? How long will we deal with that government, and what safeguards can we build in, in light of what we have been confronted with after the election in the province of Quebec, which is now governed by a separatist government? Of course the native people may argue that they cannot be any worse off than they were before, and I agree with them on that, but I would like to ask them whether, having waited 100 years, they would not want to wait two more years to check the record and see what we on this side of the House have achieved for them in the last three years. Let them check the commitments we have made to them and the policy that we have developed to deal with the very special needs throughout our country, not the special needs in northern Quebec but the needs of all our indigenous people regardless of where they live.
The James Bay agreement has brought about all these measures for the native people of northern Quebec through an agreement which takes precedence over federal, legal, constitutional and historical jurisdiction over the native people, by avoiding the creation of reserve lands which would have had a special protective status, and by leaving the entire responsibility for the native people to the province. In other words, special status or the possibility of special status for our native people will be eliminated by this agreement.
Contrary to the rhetoric of the agreement, it is purely assimilationist in its approach, and if the native people have made a commitment to assimilate and integrate into our society and if they are ready for all the consequences which will flow from that, I say the agreement is good. However, they must allow me and some of my colleagues to express some doubt.
The institutions and structures which the agreement sets up provide for non native participation in a manner which will leave most native communities defenceless in the face of a large influx of people from the south. Those native people who are unwilling or unable to assimilate will be left on the fringes as dispossessed outsiders looking in. In the circumstances it seems reasonable to expect frustration, loss of pride, hostility, and all the social, economic and psychological problems which plague many of the native communities further south.
The James Bay agreement is just as iniquitous and one sided as nineteenth century treaties which were forced on natives under former colonial regimes. Yet there is some tendency on the part of the federal government to set this agreement up as a model which can be followed in the Yukon, Northwest Territories, British Columbia and elsewhere. I am serving notice on this government right now that when this kind of
December 8, 1976

thing is proposed to the people I represent, the government will have to deal with me.
Native resistance to intrusions on to their lands will have to cease being a rearguard action if native identity and native rights are to survive into the next century. The process of extinguishing, in northern Quebec, native rights of possession and use of their lands also includes, under the agreement, the termination of existing and potential special status for these native people under the constitution and the Indian Act.
I would like to read the full text of the press release which was issued yesterday by the Native Council of Canada, which represents all those people who are not recognized under the Indian Act as being status Indians. However, they have the same problems and the same difficulties in finding their way in this complex society which we have established on this continent, finding their way into the institutions which are set up to service this society and the people within it, and finding their way into an equal partnership which they will eventually need if they wish to establish a brighter future for their future generations. I am going to read this statement because I do not think the press, which received it at twelve o'clock yesterday, has featured it in any publication which I saw this morning. That shows that neither this institution nor society as a whole is aware of the real problem. I quote from the statement as follows:
Legislation is now before the Parliament of Canada to ratify an agreement signed last year between the Cree and Inuit people of northern Quebec on the one hand, and the government of Quebec on the other. The native council believes that parliament should not move quickly to approve this agreement because of the dramatic political changes which resulted in the election of a separatist government in the province of Quebec. As matters now stand there is absolutely no guarantee that native rights can be safeguarded in the event that a new political structure is in place in Quebec two years from now.
The federal government has no right to sign over its responsibilities for Indian and Eskimo lands in any part of Canada to a jurisdiction whose avowed goal is independence from the federal authority. Previous guarantees and safeguards built into the proposed agreement are meaningless in a Quebec that may not, in the future, be part of Canada under the constitutional authority of a federal government.
The whole matter should be reviewed by a parliamentary committee, prior to second reading of the enabling legislation, for the purpose of exploring several new options:
1.	Re-examination to determine that all guarantees, safeguards and commitments undertaken by the government of Quebec will be maintained by any future political jurisdiction in Quebec.
2.	Re-negotiation of the agreement with ail native people in northern Quebec to ascertain if they wish to cede their lands and territories to a political jurisdiction committed to independence from the federal government. Logically, the native people should, at the very least, be entitled to a referendum within two years to decide their future participation in confederation.
3.	Re-assessment of the terms of the proposed agreement to ensure that the rights of the Metis and non-status Indians of the territory and several other groups of Indian people not included at present are safeguarded by any new or revised agreement that may result.
The Parliament of Canada is the guardian of the native people and the lands they occupy and cannot, under any circumstances, divest itself of federal responsibilities for these groups. A full inquiry is essential! No amount of pressure, from whatever source, should force the Parliament of Canada into a hasty ratification of an agreement that will allow the Quebec jurisdiction to extinguish rights of the native people to land they have used since time immemorial.
James Bay Agreement
I agree that the Quebec election has added a new dimension to the James Bay agreement. I endorse the statement made by the Native Council of Canada yesterday that there should be no rush to get this passed and that there is time for a sober second look at what went on in the province of Quebec. We will have to continue to safeguard the rights of native people. This government has no right to abrogate its responsibility to native people and pass it on to a province, particularly a province which has as its avowed goal separation from confederation.
How can we possibly safeguard rights and how can we insist on the provisions of this agreement if separation should in fact take place? Even if it does not, does this agreement not open the doors to a whole series of constitutional conflicts which will arise?
I wish to quote from statements made during the debate by our friend in Quebec who acted as the special representative of Premier Bourassa to negotiate on his behalf the James Bay agreement. He said this:
We have negotiated with two minorities which felt themselves threatened with extinction. The Native peoples are battling for their survival. If the state does not succeed in establishing principles aimed at assuring the survival of these minorities it could well happen that we might not even be able to guarantee our own.
He was speaking for the government of Quebec. He was concerned about the survival of his own society. What guarantee can the province of Quebec give us-even if it does not separate-that it will continue to safeguard the commitment made to our native brothers, to our friends, to the indigenous people who have lived in this country since time immemorial?
The James Bay agreement will probably be ratified, because my experience in this House teaches me that when this government has made up its mind, little happens to change it. I would warn my native brothers, however, that the waters will continue to flow, the wind will continue to blow, and the sun will continue to shine. But I wonder if the sun will shine as brightly when future generations are born as it was shining before this agreement was signed and ratified by this House. I wonder if the waters will be as clear and as sparkling as they were, after they have sold out all their rights. I wonder if the wind will be as pure and as fresh as it is now. I have my doubts, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to give a warning to my native friends. When we reassess this decision ten, 15 or 20 years from now, when the snowmobile needs a new belt and the house needs new windows, I should like to be on record as having told them of the mistake they were making.
I agree that no option was open to them. They probably achieved the best agreement possible when the gun was at their head. But, Mr. Speaker, they did not come and ask us for help when we were ready to fight for them. We offered our help and told them that together we could have achieved a better agreement. Maybe we could have delayed the project a little, but we were not asked for help. I am afraid the leaders

December 8, 1976
James Bay Agreement
who have been hailed as the authors of this agreement in this House must have been blinded by the instant prosperity offered to them. I am afraid their days will not be as bright when they try to explain what happened in the James Bay area to their children and their children's children.
I do not know what will happen to this bill in committee, Mr. Speaker, but this party is committed to some very significant amendments. I appeal again to those who negotiated the treaty to sit down with us and help us fight these amendments through the committee stage. There is still time to build in some safeguards. We respect their decision, but we seek their help because we cannot do this alone. We might need them to voice their opinion to our friends opposite, who respond to political expediency and political pressure. We will put up a fight in committee but we cannot do it alone. I am afraid this bill will pass, as does any other to which the government has put its mind. With many of my colleagues on this side of the House I consider this to be one of the dark days for all natives, all Indian people in this country.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this parliament we used to have a procedure of debating resolutions prior to the introduction of specific bills. As I listened to this debate which has been going on since last evening it seemed to me too bad that most of the speeches could not have been made before the introduction of the bill. There might have been some amendments that would have made the legislation more useful and helpful in light of the needs of the native people across Canada.
Some very interesting statements have been made, however. It is interesting that the emphasis has been on the precedent that will be established by this major initiative on the part of the government for a rather substantial land settlement. This could become the basis for future negotiations of land settlements, many of which are in process or on the horizon. I hope government supporters will enter the debate and indicate that they are just as concerned as the opposition about the needs and welfare of this very significant minority group-in fact the most important minority group of Canada, the native people. I hope that my hon. friend, the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) will enter the debate. On many occasions I have heard him say that the problem with all the native people in this country, and particularly with regard to land claims, arises from the fact that they did not have a more effective immigration policy back in the early days. If they had, of course we would not be in this parliament today discussing the important issues of native land claims.
The reason so much concern is expressed by spokesmen on the opposition side is because this country's record with respect to native land rights has not been good. There is some justification for the native people being suspicious of the motives of the present legislation. It is understandable that the Native Brotherhood presses for careful consideration of the terms of the bill. This will certainly be the posture of members of the opposition as the bill goes through the various stages.

The Brotherhood is engaged in an amendment or complete replacement of the Indian Act-which is really a white man's act for Indians as the Indians never had any input. Many of the precedents that will be established if this bill is approved will have a serious impact on the final recommendations of the Brotherhood with respect to an adequate Indian Act, one which will arise out of the input of the native people themselves.
I speak as a member from western Canada where there is a fairly substantial Indian population. There are two reservations in my constituency, both made up of the Sioux band. Long before I came into this parliament I was concerned about conditions on these reservations, and as minister for northern affairs and national resources in a previous government I found that the same situations that existed in my constituency unfortunately and tragically applied right across this great country of ours.
The initial land settlements obviously did not favour the native people who were exploited by means of treaties and material allurements which, to put it mildly, represented downright theft and hypocrisy on the part of the original negotiators of the treaties. Aboriginal rights were never dealt with in any of those treaties concerning western land settlements, as I have examined them.
Only because of the role of the RCMP, originally the North West Mounted Police, in these negotiations, a role which led to the establishment of trust and confidence among the native peoples, was it relatively easy to persuade the native peoples on the prairies to enter into totally inadequate land settlement agreements. What happened was not the fault of the RCMP. They did not do the negotiating, but they established the basis for the trust and confidence which, from the white man's viewpoint, made the successful negotiations possible. I must say that Canada's reputation in this regard is better than that of the United States, because land exploitation there was accompanied by violence, even military action. That never occurred in the wide open spaces of western Canada. I use the phrase "wide open spaces" because the particular territory involved in the agreement now before the House is an area of wide open spaces so far as population is concerned. We are considering an area the population of which is between 20,000 and 30,000 people.
Perhaps because the sense of guilt of the United States government was stronger than that of the Canadian government, authorities in that country moved more quickly than we did to deal with land claim settlements and to renegotiate land claims. They have had a land claims commission functioning for a number of years, and major land concessions and settlements have been made.
Canada attempted to follow the same pattern by adopting almost the same formula, because in 1963 there was legislation before parliament to set up a land claims commission. The idea in setting up a commission was to establish a body which would have sufficient manpower and legal expertise to apply
December 8, 1976

policies, decisions and agreements consistently right across the country. Unfortunately there was a change of government in 1963 and legislation to set up the land claims commission did not proceed. Instead the new Liberal government chose to proceed on an ad hoc basis by appointing a land claims commissioner, in the person of Dr. Barber. He has since that time been compiling information on the various land claim issues across the country.
If I may speak to the agreement before the House, I strongly agree with the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), who made an excellent presentation to the House last night. He said that we must give this issue our earnest and careful consideration because we are making major decisions about the future of a minority group in this country. And we are pausing to consider the question carefully and earnestly because of the bad record of the past, to which I briefly referred earlier. For, out of those earlier agreements came poverty, poor housing and a shocking infant mortality rate. There was ill health which resulted in a mortality rate of almost astronomical proportions when compared with rates of other parts of the community. All those things are a matter of record, and have been a matter of frequent public discussion across this country.
Because of the attitude of the Canadian government and of Canadians toward the land settlement issue, the native peoples have been exploited. But some improvements have been made in recent years; some important initiatives have come to the fore. Wishing to take the initiative, we decided to launch a massive attack on tuberculosis, a dangerous disease which was infesting our native peoples. I remembered that until 30 years ago pundits had been saying that the native problem would disappear in due course because the native people were a vanishing people, largely because of the crisis of disease. That attitude was callous, cold and cruel; but the question was mentioned in those terms just 30 or 40 years ago in this country.
Today the native people are no longer a vanishing people. Actually, they have this country's highest birth rate. It was one of the encouraging aspects of my ministerial responsibility that I should be involved in this major attack on tuberculosis; now, the disease has been practically eradicated both from the native Indian people and from the Inuit people as well.
Housing has improved; that is much to be desired. There has been major emphasis on improved housing for the native peoples. As well, the question of education has come into focus. In my constituency, at Brandon University-the Chancellor of Brandon University is present in the House in the person of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I am sure he will agree with what I shall say- major educational emphasis today is placed on native studies programs. At present some 350 native people are on course in that institution in various departments of study. They will be majoring in educational training so that they, themselves, can go out into the native communities, particularly northern communities, and become involved in the educational process
James Bay Agreement
of those native communities. These are improvements. We hope that this pattern will continue in future.
It is in the light of the new approach on the part of governments that I approach at this time the consideration of the implications of Bill C-9. It deals with major areas of concern. It will take a lot of unravelling to undo the wrongs of the early treaties on the prairies. Dr. Barber has been collecting dossiers on this matter for at least ten years. The process of settling the land agreements, trying to redress some of the wrongs that were committed in the early days, is going to be a long and tedious one.
The major areas of concern are in the northern parts of Canada. The native people, the Indians of northern or nouveau Quebec, as that part of the province of Quebec is sometimes referred to, the Indians and the Inuit of the Northwest Territories, and the Indian population of the Yukon, all these groups are now in the midst of very important and delicate negotiations on native land claims which will be influenced very strongly by the approach that this parliament takes to the legislation before us and the final decisions that will be made.
The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), who just spoke, said that we will be introducing many amendments in an attempt to improve the legislation. That is certainly true. We are hoping too that there will be some representations from native organizations and groups so there will be a direct input from that source. We are not quite convinced that the total story, presented by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) yesterday, has been brought before the House.
One of the treaty negotiations that will be strongly influenced by the decisions that are made with regard to Bill C-9 is the final resolution of treaties 8 and 11 as they apply north of the sixtieth parallel. Negotiation has been going on for a number of years. The whole thing has been brought into focus because of the Berger inquiry in connection with decisions on the pipeline along the Mackenzie River.
I remember during the time I was involved in the negotiations that we were very careful to avoid the decision where treaties 8 and 11 would be dealt with by an isolated financial settlement. It is fine to have a substantial sum of money given in a lump sum, or even over a period of time. However, to my mind that is not the best way of dealing with some of the problems that occurred in earlier land settlements which led to the degradation of the native population, one of the great shames of this country. I know there are some recommendations that it should be made on a per capita cash settlement basis, each native in the land area concerned being granted a specific cash settlement. Some have even suggested that we go back to the old reserve system. Therefore, there are all sorts of choices in this regard. In the decisions made with the natives involved in the James Bay power development area, there were some overtones of this thinking. There are patterns that have been affected by past experience. These are the patterns we want to avoid.

December 8, 1976
James Bay Agreement
For example, it was not because of the concern and the initiative of the federal government that we arrived at the present situation in so far as achieving an agreement of land claim settlements. We know it is only under pressure that the federal government has become involved in the negotiations.
Initially the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was very reluctant to acknowledge the fact of aboriginal rights. I remember a visit to northern Manitoba in 1968. At that time a power development was very much on the minds of the native people in northern Manitoba. The provincial government was going forward with a massive power development on the Churchill and Nelson Rivers. The native people, in an audience with the Prime Minister, were pressing the claims of aboriginal rights. The response of the Prime Minister at that time was that they should forget these rights and become good Canadians like the rest of us and be a part of the great Canadian community.
It was only after the Nishga settlement that the Prime Minister changed his mind. Speaking to them directly, he said perhaps they have more legal rights than we originally thought. There was not any great anxiety and concern on the part of the highest level of leadership in this country to assure, spontaneously and from a thorough knowledge of the situation, the rights of the native people with regard to the James Bay power development.
At the provincial level the decision to proceed with the development has been put before this House by at least two speakers. It was made without any reference to or negotiation with the native people in the James Bay area. It completely ignored the guarantees under the 1912 Extension of Boundaries Act. The earlier act did not even take those rights into consideration because we were still in the era which was typical of land settlements on the prairies. The white man proceeded as if it was his divine right to move in and occupy these territories.
The decision on the part of the Quebec government and the James Bay Power Corporation to go ahead with the project had been made on the basis of an election promise. This was in spite of technical advice to the contrary. I repeat that the posture of Ottawa at that time was to maintain, as the hon. member for Lambton-Kent described it last evening, alert neutrality and silence.
I know we have a new Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. Allmand). He has a reputation for humanitarian considerations. However, he was a member of the cabinet at that time and these matters would have been discussed around the cabinet table. He was also a member of parliament from the province of Quebec. Therefore he should have had particular insight into what was taking place in this regard, even back in those early days of the seventies.
It was the native people themselves who took action. One of the encouraging aspects of the whole episode is that the native people had enough knowledge, background, and gumption to get into action and call for an injunction. The decision of Mr. Justice Malouf was one of historic significance. He gave an injunction favourable to the native people of the northern part of Quebec. Since that time the native people have been able to

put forward fairly substantial material to support their position. But it should still be remembered that it has been a case almost of negotiating with a gun at their heads because both the provincial and federal governments had indicated they were going ahead, in typically irresponsible fashion, without reference to the native people at all until the people themselves took action in their own defence.
I do not intend to go into the details of the legislation; there are others who wish to take part in the debate. What concerns me is the emphasis which is placed on monetary settlements. That is fine, as long as monetary settlements are directed toward meeting the real needs of the native people-if they are to be used to establish health programs, housing programs, and educational programs which will enable the communities to avoid the degradation which arose in the early days of native land settlements. Funds could be used to ensure that natives in the area concerned will have a continuing opportunity for employment, which has not been the case in the past in the Northwest Territories or in the Yukon. Even with the best of intentions on the part of governments it has not been possible to bring the native people into the mainstream of 20th Century industrial economic life. The situation has largely been brought about by failure to understand sufficiently the real needs of the native people.
These are some of the aspects of the legislation to which I shall be giving special attention. One of the areas of concern which has already been dealt with is the transfer of responsibility from the federal to the provincial level. I believe some amendment will be needed in this regard because the course now proposed violates the fundamental protection provided for the native people in the constitution, according to which the senior level of government is ultimately responsible for the well being of the native people.
The minister makes much of the fact that most of the communities in the north have voted in favour of the agreement, but I am reminded that there are many kinds of voting. I recall talking at the United Nations to a delegate from one of the countries which happened to be behind the Iron Curtain. He was a gentleman very learned in jurisprudence, and I told him I was amazed that he followed so supinely in his voting activities the directions of a certain power which had strong influence on his delegation-I am not mentioning countries or persons, I am merely illustrating a principle. He defended himself by saying, "You in the western democracies misunderstand what is happening behind the Iron Curtain. You boast about the secret ballot. When you vote, only you know who or what you are voting for. Behind the Iron Curtain we have carried that procedure to a far higher level of secrecy. When we vote, we do not even know who or want we are voting for." I am just wondering how much of that guided democracy has gone into the decision made by the native people in this regard. If it is that sort of direction, by handing out monetary rewards, I think it is the worst kind of paternalism and should be avoided at any cost.
December 8, 1976

At this stage of the discussion nothing more needs to be said. We have expressed our concern. This is a precedent which can have enormous significance for the other land claim issues which are before the people and the Government of Canada at the moment, and we want to make sure that in every respect and by all possible means the rights and privileges of the native people will be respected right down to dotting the last "i" and crossing the last "t".

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us this afternoon a bill which marks another sad chapter in the history of negotiations between the white man and the native people of Canada. As my hon. friend from the Northwest Territories stated in the debate last night, we in the NDP have serious reservations about Bill C-9, the manner in which the James Bay agreement was brought about, and the implications for future land settlements in this country.
Bill C-9 sets an important precedent, and will cost the native people a very high price. The native people in the area saw the tremendous injustice of what was done to them, and when I hear them tell their story I am reminded very strongly of a Biblical parable. We read in the Book of Genesis that those who lived in the Garden of Eden lived in harmony with their environment. Look at the people of James Bay and see how they have been in harmony with their environment, respecting the land and adapting to what it provides for them. They have protected it well, and the environment in turn has treated them well. Listen to statements such as one made by a great trapper, Joe Bearskin, who says:
This land is our garden. In this garden, things grow and multiply. The Indians are one of the things which grow there. We all love our garden.
Observations such as these bring home to those of us who live in the white community how important hunting, fishing and trapping rights are to native people who need those rights not only as a means of sustenance but also as a means of preserving their ancient culture and identity as a people who use only what they need, so that the land and the animals on it may replenish themselves. The land is their livelihood. It is an insurance policy not only for themselves and their children but for their children's children. It is a very precious element of their culture. Faraway governments here and in Quebec City are making decisions which will affect these people not only today but for generations to come.
This James Bay development is a modern day flood affecting the people in that area in no less dimension than the flood of ancient times as recorded in the Book of Genesis. We have here in the James Bay development proposal in northern Quebec a project that will flood an area of over 20,000 square miles, larger than Nova Scotia. It will divert numerous rivers; it will destroy fish spawning grounds; it will destroy wild fowl nesting areas and the habitat of animals; it will alter the migration of many animals, the deer, the moose and the caribou; it will divert the food resources of the natives, and in
James Bay Agreement
many respects force many to rely on alternative means of subsistence, the white man's food, for which the native people must pay cash. It is a flood that will cover potential mineral and forest reserves. It is a flood of immense proportions. As one of the residents, a trapper by the name of William Matoush, says:
When we don't kill so many beaver as we could, it is like putting something away in the bank. The beaver are our savings. Now if the white man is going to come and flood the land he is wiping out our savings.
We have a new flood; a flood designed coldly and calculatingly by the James Bay Development Corporation. The repercussions are going to be immense. As one anthropologist, Dr. Richard Salisbury of McGill University, reported, after leading a task force study of the area:
Any reduction of the supply of bush foods would clearly have an effect on the economy of the local people, especially in terms of the quality of the diet.
The replacement of a high quality meat diet by a diet of low quality store-bought carbohydrates is a phenomenon that has been reported throughout the Third World as a reaction to urbanization, and that has seriously lowered health and nutritional standards . . .
Existing levels of cash earnings and transfer payments are tolerable while costs for food can be kept at a minimum and diet kept at a high quality through hunting ... Once subsistence hunting is let go, the northern people are involved in a downward spiral of dependency, with wages in the north never catching up with the built-in inflation of prices in the area.
Faced with this modern day flood, what is the ark that the Cree and Inuit of James Bay are forced to take refuge in? What kind of alternative salvation to the massive development project is there that they have to accept? It is known as the James Bay Corporation, or the James Bay treaty as it really turns out to be, and the complementary legislation in this federal parliament, Bill C-9.
In return for this development the native people of the area have been forced to give up their aboriginal rights over a huge territory they have been using since time immemorial. In return they are granted small reserves, or land analogous to reserves. They are given temporary guarantees of exclusive hunting rights in the surrendered part of the territory until such time as it is needed for occupation and settlement by white society. They are given local government and control over education, administration and justice, and they are also given a cash settlement, as in the old treaties; a cash settlement of approximately $10 million a year for the next 20 years, or a cash settlement that works out to about $1.50 per acre of the land that has been signed away. That is the ark; that is the refuge that the native people have been forced into because of the flood of the modern day James Bay development.
I use the word "forced" because that is what has happened. The native people were forced into accepting the settlement and not given time to negotiate the best kind of deal possible for the people in the area. Certainly once their injunction against the project had been overturned in the courts it appeared inevitable that they had no alternative but to accept the proposal put forward by the James Bay Development Corporation. There were no meaningful negotiations, in my opinion, in the entire history of this development. There were

December 8, 1976
James Bay Agreement
token negotiations. It was made to appear that the Indian and Inuit people were being consulted.
When you look at the history of this sad case of white exploitation of the people in the area, I do not see how anyone could conclude that negotiations were in any way meaningful or just, because at the same time that supposed real negotiations were taking place between the native people and the James Bay Development Corporation, that same corporation was beginning construction on native land without native permission. In other words, they were proceeding on a course that would present the original inhabitants of that area with a fait accompli. It soon became apparent to the Cree and the Inuit people of the area that it would be a fruitless course to proceed further in the courts to halt the project after Justice MalouPs decision or injunction granting a temporary halt to the development was overturned.
The courts definitely appeared unsympathetic. The federal government, which should have been acting on the natives' behalf, was becoming impatient. There were veiled threats to withdraw the federal funding that was helping the native people conduct their research and other support activities.
The history of the development in that area, without meaningful consultation and without giving the native people time to do all the necessary environmental and economical assessment, is indeed a sad one. Let us briefly look at the series of events which illustrate how meaningless the negotiations were, and how the native people always had their backs to the wall.
In April of 1971 the Quebec Liberal government first announced the grandiose James Bay project. In July of that same year a number of Indian chiefs of the James Bay area petitioned the federal government to stop the project. No action was taken by the federal government. This was the first sign that the federal government was abrogating its responsibilities under the British North America Act and subsequent legislation to have a direct input into this development because it affected native people.
The Indian Act, the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act of 1912, the Fisheries Act, the Navigable Waters Protection Act, and the Canada Water Act-any of these instruments could have been used by the federal government to get the government involved in the project, so it could demand of the government of Quebec that the project be halted until meaningful studies had been done by the native people, and alternative proposals to the James Bay development projects as then conceived could be presented. But there was no such action on the part of the federal Liberal government. It sat back and delegated its responsibility to a provincial government that was closing its ears to the pleas of the native people in the area that elementary justice be done.
By the end of 1971, Mr. Speaker, work had begun on the project without consultation with the native people. By January 6, 1973, 175 miles of access roads had been completed, and contracts had been let for the remaining 260 miles. In June, 1973, docks and wharves had been built on Fort Georgia

Island ready to receive heavy equipment. The first dam reservoir was built at site LG-2, delivery of the equipment was completed by April, 1973, construction of the portals begun by May, 1973, and tunnel construction was begun in October, 1973. All of this preparatory work, moving of equipment and commitment of money, was undertaken before any settlement had been reached with the native people. The native people were being forced to negotiate with a gun to their heads; they could see the development already starting in the area, without any formal authorization or a treaty having been signed. Not only was construction of the dams begun, but by 1973, 20,000 tons of equipment and material had been moved into the area; in 1974 the amount increased to 75,000 tons. Planning was also under way for transmission lines.
That illustrates, Mr. Speaker, what was going on and the kind of intense pressure that was being put on the native people. In fact they were presented with a fait accompli. They were told "You can negotiate according to what we, the James Bay Development Corporation, want in terms of a timetable; or you can refuse to negotiate and the project will go ahead anyway." What kind of meaningful negotiation and elementary justice is that, Mr. Speaker?
So on one hand we have a $16 billion hydroelectric project, all the might and talent available to the huge corporate interests which were pushing ahead with the project; on the other hand, you have a few thousand native people caught off guard, expected to do in a few months the kind of research and prepare the kind of case that it had taken these companies three years to do prior to 1971. At the same time the native people were given a deadline; they had to sign an agreement by November 1, 1975.
The native people were in the process of negotiating away their birthright, not with the Government of Canada-as was the obligation under the legislation-not directly with the government of Quebec, but with a Crown corporation. What kind of indication is this of the seriousness and respect that white governments show the native people in the area? It is a very sad commentary indeed.
The native people were given two years to complete their study on land use and the environmental effects of the project. I suggest the period was completely inadequate. At the same time that they were supposed to complete their study the project was pushing ahead. Construction of the dams was proceeding, and equipment was moving into the area. How could there be a real consultative process going on with the people of the area who were scattered across a vast region in small communities, many out on the traplines? How could the implications of this complicated agreement be brought home to all these people in time? There is no human or physical way that that could be done.
I am convinced that the treaty will be viewed by future generations as a tragedy, as an illustration of how the people of the day in that area were forced, without any real option at their disposal, to sign away their birthright. I hope that the provisions in the bill, some of which are commendable in terms of granting more local autonomy and giving opportunity for
December 8, 1976

development of the native people, will offset what I see as the great disadvantage, but 1 am pessimistic that they will. So in view of the terms of the bill and what they mean for the future of the people of the James Bay area, I can only conclude that their future is rather pessimistic unless there is a real change in the way governments from this point on start to honour their agreements and commitments, and begin to treat Canada's first citizens in a just and fair manner.
The ramifications of the James Bay development must certainly go beyond simply native rights. I question the project not only on social, legal and humane grounds, but also on economic grounds. First of all, there has been no adequate environmental study done on the effect of the flooding of the area. There has been no complete environmental study done on the ecosystems, not only in the immediate James Bay area but in areas beyond the actual project itself. The project will have severe ramifications for northern Quebec and northeastern Ontario.
No studies have been done into what this massive flooding will do to the climate of the region. It could be altered immeasurably and have consequences not only for the people of the immediate area but for southern Quebec and elsewhere, in the form of a climatic change that would affect crops, snowfall or rain. Surely with a project of this magnitude we should expect a thorough environmental analysis, but one has not been done.
So far as the financing of this $16 billion project is concerned, many serious questions remain unanswered-for example, the actual cost allocation and the ramifications of the cost upon the Canadian economy. Money has had to be borrowed from outside Canada to help finance this project, but the interest, of course, has to be paid by Canadian taxpayers. The importation of vast amounts of capital for the James Bay area is surely one of the factors which have put pressure on the Canadian dollar and caused its recent devaluation, with all kinds of implications of higher import prices on products used by Canadians.
The question has to be asked whether the $16 billion, or portions of it, could not have been far better spent on alternative energy development rather than on going into such a huge debt to provide hydro-electric power from the James Bay development.
The other question is, who will be the primary beneficiaries of this hydro-electric power? My understanding is that most of it will be exported to the United States. We have to consider also that under the vast areas that are flooded there are potential mineral resources that will be lost forever in terms of possible future royalties to some of the native people who have territorial land claims over it or for development for future Canadian use.
When I look at the James Bay project, I must ask myself whether we have learnt anything from our experience with the Columbia River Treaty and the kind of environmental and economic disaster which that development has proved to be for
James Bay Agreement
Canada and for our future. I think that historians down the line will rank the James Bay project as a debacle much greater and much more severe in its repercussions than the mistakes made with the Columbia River Treaty.
I am saying that the James Bay hydro electric project is a mistake for economic, environmental and social reasons. I say that Bill C-9 which is before us today ratifies this agreement at the cost to the native people of losing forever their traditional enshrined rights, because in clause 3(3) of the bill we read the following:
All native claims, rights, title and interests, whatever they may be, in and to the Territory, of all Indians and all Inuit, wherever they may be, and all the native claims, rights, title and interests whatever they may be, in Canada, of all the Inuit of Port Burwell are hereby extinguished ...
That is a tremendous price to pay for the people of that area for the sake of hydro-electric power for white communities in southern Canada and the United States. Surely if this government and its Quebec counterpart had been serious about developing the area, they could have done so and provided compensation to the native people without requiring them to give up forever their aboriginal rights. That is what we object to most about this settlement.
I cannot impress upon the House enough that this James Bay project, by flooding such huge areas of land and by altering so much of the environment in terms of the river systems and the animal habitat, is of such immense proportions to the people living there. We in our society, I am afraid, do not understand or comprehend how important the land is to the people of that area and why they should have some future claim to use it in order to provide not only an economic livelihood but a cultural identity as well.
I refer hon. members for their reading to a report by Peter J. Usher who was a consultant to the Inuit Tapirisat of Canada. This report dates back to April 6, 1973, and it was prepared mainly in the context of the native people in the Northwest Territories, but the sentiment and the implications are certainly the same for the people living in the James Bay area. I should like to quote briefly from Mr. Usher's report. He writes:
To native people, the land is more than just a source of food or cash. It is the permanent source of their security and of their sense of well being. It is the basis of what they are as people. The land, and the birds, fish and animals it supports, have sustained them and their ancestors since time immemorial. Properly cared for, it can always do so. Native people know how to take care of the land, and they know why that must be done.
We can offer them jobs, but the history of the Northwest Territories, of northern Quebec and of any area where we have offered native people jobs has usually been a boom or bust cycle. When the bust occurs and the jobs disappear, the white people in the area can always move south, back into the white culture, the white society, but where do the native people go when there are no more jobs and they have given up forever their rights to the land?
That is why we in this party disagree with Bill C-9 because it says that the people of that area must forever give up the rights to the land that they have had to this date. I do not trust this government nor the government of Quebec to honour the

December 8, 1976
James Bay Agreement
subsequent guarantees in the James Bay agreement or in Bill C-9, and to honour other compensation that the native people have negotiated in return for giving up those rights.
In my opinion this is a bad agreement signed by the native people under duress. Bill C-9 is a bad bill because it extinguishes native rights in return for questionable guarantees, and it sets a bad precedent for future land claim settlements in Canada. The federal government has failed in its responsibility to see that justice is done and due process of the law is followed for the native people. It has failed in its responsibility to .uphold basic human rights, and neither 1 nor my party want to be a part of this decision, and so we will vote against the bill.
